title: Mental models
description: Thinking tools you can name, explain and reach for when a decision gets hard.

ideas.title: Reasoning from the ground up
ideas.summary: Break a problem down to what must be true, or turn it around and ask what would guarantee failure.

items.q: What does it mean to reason from first principles?
items.a: To break a problem down to its most basic truths and build up from them, rather than copying what was done before

items.q: Which mental model solves a problem backwards, by asking what would guarantee failure and then avoiding it?
items.a: Inversion

items.q: Which 19th-century mathematician's maxim "invert, always invert" did Charlie Munger make famous as a thinking habit?
items.a: Carl Jacobi

items.q: What is a premortem, the planning exercise devised by the psychologist Gary Klein?
items.a: Imagining that the project has already failed and working out why, before it starts

ideas.title: The razors
ideas.summary: Razors are rules of thumb that shave away unlikely explanations: prefer the simpler one, and the less sinister.

items.q: Which razor says that, among explanations that fit the facts, you should prefer the one with the fewest assumptions?
items.a: Occam's razor

items.q: Which razor says never to attribute to malice what is adequately explained by carelessness or stupidity?
items.a: Hanlon's razor

items.q: What does Hitchens's razor say about a claim that is asserted without evidence?
items.a: It can be dismissed without evidence

items.q: A colleague has not answered your email for three days. What does Hanlon's razor tell you to assume before assuming a snub?
items.a: That they are busy, forgot or missed it: carelessness, not malice

items.q: Occam's razor is named for William of Ockham, an English friar of which century?
items.a: The 14th century

ideas.title: Map and territory
ideas.summary: Every model simplifies reality; it is useful only as far as it matches the ground, and no further.

items.q: Who coined the phrase "the map is not the territory"?
items.a: Alfred Korzybski

items.q: What does the saying "the map is not the territory" warn against?
items.a: Confusing a model or description of reality with reality itself

items.q: Which statistician wrote that "all models are wrong, but some are useful"?
items.a: George Box

items.q: What is a circle of competence, the idea Warren Buffett applies to investing?
items.a: The area you truly understand; the skill is knowing where its edge is and staying inside it

ideas.title: Second-order thinking
ideas.summary: Ask "and then what?" because the consequences of consequences often matter more than the first effect.

items.q: What is second-order thinking?
items.a: Considering the consequences of the consequences, not just the immediate effect

items.q: What does Chesterton's fence advise before you remove a rule or structure whose purpose you cannot see?
items.a: First find out why it was put there

items.q: What is the cobra effect?
items.a: An incentive that makes the problem worse; named for a story of a cobra bounty that led people to breed cobras

items.q: Which law says that "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"?
items.a: Goodhart's law

items.q: A city widens a road to ease traffic; the easier drive attracts more cars until it is jammed again. What is this second-order effect called?
items.a: Induced demand

ideas.title: Odds, payoffs and base rates
ideas.summary: Good decisions weigh how likely each outcome is and how much it matters, starting from how often such things happen.

items.q: How do you work out the expected value of a bet?
items.a: Multiply each outcome's value by its probability, then add the results

items.q: A bet pays $100 with a 10% chance and nothing otherwise. What is its expected value?
In reasoning about probability, what is a base rate?
items.a: How often something happens in general in the relevant group, before you look at the particular case

items.q: What does the Pareto principle, or 80/20 rule, say?
items.a: Roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes

items.q: What is a margin of safety, in engineering and in investing?
items.a: A buffer between what you expect and what you can survive, so that errors do not ruin you

items.q: What does regression to the mean predict after an unusually extreme result?
items.a: With imperfectly correlated repeated measurements, an extreme result tends to be followed by one closer to the mean
